idiom_name: Spring Security AuthorizationManager behind AuthorizationFilter (request level)
implementation_notes: Spring Security supplies both halves and names them: AuthorizationFilter is the enforcement point and AuthorizationManager is the decision point. The request DSL authorises by pattern and method with authorizeHttpRequests(...) - using anyRequest().denyAll() as the catch-all turns the rule set into an allow list - and the filter throws AccessDeniedException, which ExceptionTranslationFilter converts into 403. Implement a custom AuthorizationManager only when the decision needs data the DSL cannot express (a policy service or an authorization database); controllers must never test roles themselves.
pitfalls: AuthorizationFilter is last in the chain by default: filters registered before it are not covered by these rules, and Spring MVC endpoints are only covered if they are matched explicitly.
Method security is opt-in per annotation: unannotated methods stay unsecured, so a request-level catch-all rule has to back it up.

Reading SecurityContextHolder from a thread started by the application (or an async dispatch without inherited context) loses the Authentication and either fails the decision or resolves it against the wrong subject.

variants.name: Request-level DSL (authorizeHttpRequests + AuthorizationFilter)
Method-level annotations (@EnableMethodSecurity + @PreAuthorize)
variants.implementation_notes: With @EnableMethodSecurity, annotated methods and classes are guarded by AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor, which evaluates the SpEL expression through PreAuthorizeAuthorizationManager and throws AccessDeniedException on a negative decision (surfaced as 403 by ExceptionTranslationFilter in a web request). This is the fine-grained realization: the expression sees method parameters and return values (@PostAuthorize, @PreFilter/@PostFilter exist for the result side), at the cost of rules living on the method declaration instead of in one policy block - and unannotated methods are not secured, so a request-level catch-all rule must remain.
pitfalls: Annotation-based method security leaves unannotated methods open: declare a catch-all request rule for the whole application.
@PostAuthorize runs after the method body, so a database write that has already happened cannot be undone by the denial - read first, then write.
Self-invocation (this.otherMethod()) bypasses the proxy, so the security interceptor never runs.
